text: Flash, burn marks, short shots, parts that stick. Often, the cause isn't the process. It's the mould.
Here's how an injection mould works, and how to look after it.
Mould preventive maintenance.
This is a two-plate, cold-runner mould with four cavities, clamped between the fixed and moving platens of the machine.
On the fixed half, the locating ring centres the mould on the platen, and the nozzle seals against the sprue bushing.
The cavity plate forms the outside of each part. The core plate, on the moving half, forms the inside. They meet at the parting line.
Guide pillars and bushes line the two halves up, before the steel faces touch.
The mould clamps shut. Melt is injected down the sprue, along the runners, and through small gates into the cavities.
The air in each cavity has to get out ahead of the melt. It escapes through vents ground into the parting line, just a few hundredths of a millimetre deep.
Deep enough for air. Too shallow for plastic.
Water flows through cooling channels around each cavity, connected with fittings and sealed with O-rings. It carries the heat away. Cooling is usually the longest part of the cycle.
Then the mould opens. The parts stay on the cores, and the sprue puller pulls the sprue out of the bushing.
Behind the core plate, between the spacer blocks, the ejector plates move forward. Ejector pins push the parts off the cores, and they drop clear.
Return pins and springs bring the ejector plates back, and the mould closes for the next shot.
A busy mould repeats this cycle hundreds of thousands of times a year.
And every cycle leaves something behind.
Gas and residue build up in the vents. When a vent blocks, the trapped air is squeezed so hard that it scorches the plastic. That's deezeling, and it leaves burn marks.

text: Or the air holds the melt back, and the cavity never fills. A short shot.
Scale and rust narrow the cooling channels. Less water flows, hot spots form, and the cycle has to get longer to cool the parts.
Guide pillars and bushes wear. The halves no longer line up, the parting line gets damaged, and plastic squeezes out as flash.
Ejector pins gall and stick, or snap, and parts hang up on the core.
Residue plates out on the cavity surface. Hardened O-rings leak, and water creeps out onto the parting line.
And a chilled mould, left standing in humid air, sweats. Condensation forms on the steel, and rust follows.
Warning signs: flash, burn marks, and short shots.
Parts sticking or dragging, and noisy ejection.
Water at the parting line, and cavities running at different temperatures.
And the cycle time creeping up.
So: plan maintenance by shot count, not just by the calendar.
Every shift, on the press: clean the parting line and the vents, check for water leaks, and lightly grease the guide pins.
At each periodic service, open up the ejector half. Clean and lubricate the pins, check the springs, and measure the vent depths.
Descale and flow-test every cooling circuit, and fit new O-rings.
At a longer interval, strip the whole mould down. Record every service on the mould history card, with the shot count.
Before storage, blow the water lines dry, protect the steel with rust preventive, and store the mould closed.
Follow the tool owner's maintenance spec, and never modify the mould without approval. After every service, check the first-off parts.
Clean vents. Free pins. Good parts.
